                                  PUC PROJECT NO. 58482

                                              §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD DEMAND                             §
MANAGEMENT SERVICE                            §                     OF TEXAS

                     VISTRA CORPORATE SERVICES COMPANY’S
                   COMMENTS IN RESPONSE TO STAFF'S OUESTIONS

TO THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Vistra Corporate Services Company (Vistra) files these Comments in response to the set
of questions for comment published by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)
Staff on March 23, 2026 relating to the implementation of PURA § 39.170. These comments are
timely filed. As requested, the executive summary is included in a separate attachment at the end
of the comments.


 1.    Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a
       seasonal service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and
       why?

       Vistra recommends that the Commission consider an as-needed service to implement
PURA § 39.170(b). Vistra recommends the Commission consider a service that is procured a
limited time in advance (such as after an Advance Action Notice is issued), rather than
seasonally. When it added PURA § 39.170(b), the Texas Legislature created a reliability
service that could be used in the event of an anticipated load-shed condition to minimize the
probability of load-shed under such circumstances. This specific goal should be considered in
tandem with consideration for the costs to customers of procuring the service and the ability of
Load Serving Entities (LSEs), such as Retail Electric Providers (REPs) to hedge or at least
reasonably anticipate the cost. An as-needed service option will help to narrow the procurement
so that LSEs, and in turn, customers are not burdened with the cost of unnecessary procurement
of the service. To that end, the Commission may want to consider a hybrid approach that
collects funds on a consistent and self-leveling basis from which the procurement budget can
be drawn down when needed, which would provide greater cost certainty and avoid surprise
uplift costs to LSEs.


Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                              Page 1
  2.    PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a
       reliability service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency
       condition. PURA § 39. l 70(b)(I) states the rules governing the new service must specify
       the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during
       extreme weather events.

         a.      Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
                 other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

       No. PURA § 39.170(b) and (b)(1) together specifically state that the service is to be
deployed in specified periods in anticipation of an emergency conditions related to an extreme
weather event.

        b.       Should the commission define "extreme weather event'' and, if so, how
                 should it be defined?

       The Commission should not define “extreme weather event,” but should give ERCOT
some guidance on event-driven procurement and deployment of the service to leverage existing
processes to the greatest extent feasible.

       The actual procurement during an event (presuming event-driven procurement) could
mimic the current ERCOT process for issuance of an Advance Action Notice (AAN) and
Outage Adjustment Evaluation (OAE)/Outage Schedule Adjustment (OSA), and follow in
sequence if ERCOT issues an AAN/OAE/OSA (which may not occur in all extreme weather
events), possibly in combination with other criteria.

       Deployment should be tied to the issuance of a Power Outage Alert for the ERCOT
region under 16 TAC § 25.57. For example, a reasonable condition precedent would be
ERCOT’s notification to the Executive Director under 16 TAC § 25.57(d), which includes
scenarios where ERCOT’s 48-hour forecast indicates system-wide generation supply
insufficiency to meet demand. If, in that example, the forecasted supply and demand balance
has not improved within 24 hours of notifying the Executive Director of such a condition and
system-wide load shed still appears likely absent the use of additional reliability services, that
would be an appropriate time to provide a deployment notification to the procured large load


Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                                Page 2
 demand management service loads.

        Leveraging existing processes will help to ensure that redundant methods are not
reinvented, leading to overall efficient implementation and coordinated deployment of the
service along with other reliability tools.



  3.    PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
        participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale
        price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that Otherwise participates in a
        different reliability or ancillary service. PURA § 37.056 l(e)-which allows ERCOT
        to direct a large load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its
        load or deploy its backup generation under certain circumstances-states that a
        large load customer with onsite backup generation may participate in a service
        authorized by PURA § 39.170(b).

         a.     What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
                customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

        The 24-hour notice is a direction from the statute. It is not related to any technical ramp
down capability of the large load, and the intent is to provide sufficient notice to participating
large load to configure their site sufficiently to meet the needs of deployment by the end of the
24-hour deployment notice window. The large load need not prove that it requires 24 hours to
ramp down safely, rather only demonstrate that it is capable of safely ramping down within 24
hours of a deployment notice (and that it is not otherwise subject to administrative
disqualification or other participation restriction penalties).

         b.     What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39. l 70(b), if any,
                should apply to participation in the new service?

        Consistent with PURA §§ 38.074 and 39.170(a)(2), as well as 16 TAC § 25.52(h)(2),
the Commission should prohibit critical natural gas facilities from participating in the new
service. This is to ensure that such loads are not incentivized to curtail during those extreme
weather events, which could risk grid reliability due to fuel supply shortage at natural gas-



Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                                 Page 3
 fueled generating facilities.

        c.     Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as
               four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude
               participation in the new service?

       It depends. The first order assumption that the 4CP or any successor transmission cost
allocation methodology reflects price responsiveness to transmission scarcity is not axiomatic.
There are certainly principles of cost causation that are aspired to in transmission cost
allocation, but transmission scarcity can be driven by multiple reliability, economic, and policy
factors that extend well beyond the average of the top coincident load intervals in each summer
month. Second, it is premature to presume what successor transmission cost allocation
methodology might look like and how that cost allocation will translate to large loads through
utility tariffs (which is the real “price responsiveness” motivator that this question is probing).

       Rather than opining on whether large load “participating” in 4CP or a successor
methodology should categorically disqualify a large load from participating in the new service,
the Commission should evaluate whether the large load exhibits behavior that would hinder its
ability to reliably perform during periods when the large load may be awarded the new service.
That may or may not overlap with the transmission cost allocation methodology, but this will
help to ensure that qualified MW is available for deployment, if called upon. Awarded large
loads would presumably already be receiving stand-by payment for the qualified MW, and
hence load curtailments to achieve any other purpose would effectively be an imputed “double
payment” for the same behavior.

        d.     Should the commission define ''curtailment in response to wholesale price
               of electricity'' and, if so, how should it be defined?

       The current definition of Controllable Load Resources (CLR) in ERCOT Protocol
Section 2 is probably the most clearly within scope for the definition of “curtailment in
response to wholesale price of electricity” and should be counted as such. Loads providing
Ancillary Services are also responsive to the wholesale price of electricity (and would
presumably be ineligible for an award under the new service and an Ancillary Service award
for the same obligation period). Similarly, other demand response or load management



Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                                   Page 4
 programs (such as the Emergency Response Service (ERS) or programs administered under the
TDUs’ Energy Efficiency auspices) may not be as directly linked to the wholesale price of
electricity but as a matter of practice are deployed when the wholesale price of electricity is
most likely elevated due to scarcity conditions, and could also be considered within the
definition of “curtailment in response to wholesale price of electricity.” Beyond those examples
of what may be inclusive to the definition, the Commission has fairly broad authority to define
that criterion with one statutory exception – a large load customer with “on-site backup
generating facilities” as defined in PURA § 37.0561(e) cannot be prohibited from participating
in the new service authorized by PURA § 39.170(b).1 This applies to all large loads, including
large loads subject to PURA § 39.169 that have such on-site backup generating facilities.



    4.   How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

         The target quantity should be based on the available budget, and as noted above in
response to Question 1, the Commission may want to pursue a “hybrid” procurement and
deployment approach that utilizes a consistent and self-leveling fee to fund a procurement
budget pool. Thus, the budget would be capped by available funds on-hand, and the quantity
procured would then become a function of offers received and the clearing price for that
particular procurement event. The Commission and ERCOT may want to subdivide the self-
leveling budget pool to allow for multiple procurements in relatively short succession as well.

         Determining that self-leveling budget pool allowance value could be done a number of
ways and Vistra offers a few considerations but does not make a specific recommendation for
that value at this time. Vistra does, however, have concerns about the potential “high side” of
the procurement costs that may not be in balance with ERCOT’s energy-only market structure.

         For example, in Project No. 55837 (Review Of Value Of Lost Load In The ERCOT
Market), the Commission set the Value Of Lost Load (VOLL) for the ERCOT market at
$35,000 per MWh. This value represents an average representative cost that consumers would
incur as a result of an unplanned outage. For non-residential consumers, the study considered

1
  See specifically PURA § 37.0561(e)(2): “This subsection does not […] prohibit a large load customer from
participating in a service authorized by Section 39.170(b).”



Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                                      Page 5
 aspects such as lost revenues, impacts on labor-related costs, damage to equipment, material
damage or spoilage, and savings on wages, unused materials, and fuel or electricity in the
determination. One natural assumption might be to set the budget pool allowance based on
VOLL coupled with the potential deployment duration of the new service. However, this
approach can drive up the total potential cost tremendously (for instance, 5,000 MW procured
assuming a 48-hour deployment window and $35,000/MWh VOLL could quickly total
5,000 x 48 x $35,000 = $8.4 billion; by comparison, the IMM’s 2024 State of the Market
Report estimated the annual aggregate costs of the ERCOT wholesale market in 2024 at
$14.2 billion2). Thus, relying only on this kind of bookend would result in adding significant
uplift cost to customer bills, and that out-of-market payment would do little to nothing to
support better in-market balance of supply and demand.

         The alternative “hybrid” method described previously could use a flat $/MWh charge to
set a practical limit on the budget for the new Service. The cost could be uplifted to all loads –
so if the fee were set at something like $0.05/MWh, then in a year like 2024 that saw
461.6 TWh of load, the program would have accrued ~$23 million that could be used towards
an event-driven procurement; if no event occurred, then the fund would continue to accrue up
to an aggregate limit. Vistra takes no position on the aggregate limit at this time, but highlights
that this approach would favor cost certainty over budget certainty, which may be a more
appropriate step while trying to establish a new service for a largely untested load resource
pool. After a few qualification/procurement rounds, ERCOT will likely be able to better
estimate the willingness of different quantities of load willing to participate each year.



    5.   What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation
         of PURA § 39.170(b)?

         Implementation of the new service needs to be properly integrated with the ERCOT
market policy framework to mitigate any unintended long-term reliability consequences. Any
deployment associated with the Service needs to be accounted for in Real-Time price formation
through accurate representation in the Reliability Deployment Price Adder (RDPA). Given the
2
 See Table A1, p. A-3 of the 2024 State of the Market Report for the ERCOT Electricity Markets, Potomac
Economics (July 2025).



Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                                   Page 6
 potential size of loads being deployed and the longer timeframe over which they will be
deployed, the RDPA should be reviewed to determine whether its accuracy could be improved
through integration of real-time telemetry, ramp rate integration, and other attributes of large
loads deployed through the new service. An under-estimated RDPA will lead to an overall
degradation of market investment signals; as the number of out-of-market actions in the
ERCOT market seem to multiply, it is all the more critical that the market distortions caused by
those out-of-market actions be responsibly mitigated.



 6.    PURA § 39.l70(a) states: The commission shall require the independent
       organization certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure
       that each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally
       owned utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including
       the installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the customer is
       interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric
       cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall
       confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated
       manner. This subsection applies only to a load interconnected after December 31,
       2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical load industrial customer, as defined
       by Section 17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical natural gas facility under Section
       38.074. Should the Commission include in this rulemaking a directive implementing
       PURA § 39.170(a)?

       The Commission will have to provide direction to ERCOT to implement
PURA § 39.170(a), either in this rulemaking or some other forum. Vistra is indifferent to
whether that occurs in this project or another; Vistra’s primary concern is that the protocols
required by PURA § 39.170(a) be coordinated with other load curtailment provisions in statute,
PUCT rules, and ERCOT’s Protocols/Guides, as the load shed curtailment protocols required by
PURA § 39.170(a) will not exist in a vacuum.

       For example, large loads subjected to curtailment conditions or commitments under
PURA §§ 37.0561(e) & 39.169(d) requirements will already be curtailed or utilizing backup
generation by the time any load shed protocols under PURA § 39.170(a) are activated, and


Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                              Page 7
 therefore need not be included in the scope of PURA § 39.170(a) implementation. Additionally,
ERCOT Planning Guide Section 9.2.5 establishes required interconnection equipment that could
be used by applicable Transmission Owner or, if the large load is co-located with a Generation
Resource, the applicable QSE, to isolate a large load from the ERCOT system, if required.

       Staff, ERCOT, and stakeholders should work to define processes specific to different
configurations of large load projects to ensure various load shed and/or load curtailment
directives are appropriately represented and accurately reflected in the RDPA when called upon.



                                       CONCLUSION
       Vistra appreciates the Commission's consideration of these comments and looks forward
to working with the Commission, Staff, ERCOT, and other stakeholders in this project.



Dated: April 8, 2026



                                                   Respectfully submitted,




                                                   Ned Bonskowski
                                                   Vice President, Texas Regulatory Policy

                                                   1005 Congress Ave., Suite 750
                                                   Austin, TX 78701

                    VISTRA’S COMMENTS - EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

1.   Vistra suggests the Commission implement an as-needed reliability service under
     PURA § 39.170(b), to be procured when necessary. This meets the goal of minimizing the
     probability of load-shed during anticipated events, while balancing customer cost
     considerations. Vistra also recommends a hybrid funding approach to ensure cost
     certainty and avoid unexpected charges for Load Serving Entities (LSEs) and customers.

2.   PURA § 39.170(b) and (b)(1) together specifically state that the service is to be deployed
     in specified periods in the event of anticipated emergency conditions related to extreme
     weather events.

3.   The Commission should avoid defining “extreme weather event,” but guide ERCOT on
     event-based procurement and deployment leveraging existing notification and adjustment
     processes. Vistra suggests procurement be modeled on (and sequenced after, as
     applicable) the Advance Action Notice/Outage Adjustment Evaluation/Outage Scheule
     Adjustment process, possibly in combination with other criteria. Deployment should be
     triggered only after the Commission’s Executive Director has been notified of a potential
     Power Outage Alert under 16 TAC § 25.57(d). These recommendations will help ensure
     efficient, coordinated use of reliability services.

4.   The Commission should not qualify large loads based on whether they require 24 hours to
     ramp down safely, but only whether they are capable of safely ramping down within 24
     hours of a deployment notice.

5.   The Commission should prohibit critical natural gas facilities from participating in the
     new service.

6.   “Participation” in 4CP or a successor transmission cost allocation methodology is too
     narrow in focus and difficult to predict as the Commission is considering changes to that
     methodology. Instead, the Commission should evaluate whether the large load exhibits
     behavior that would hinder its ability to reliably perform during periods when the large
     load may be awarded the new service.

7.   The Target procurement quantity should be based on the available budget and offers
     received. Vistra suggests a “hybrid” approach that uses a consistent, self-leveling fee to
     fund a capped budget pool (but does not opine on the appropriate size of that pool at this
     time). This would allow procurement quantities to be dictated by available funds and
     market offers, and the budget could be subdivided for multiple procurements in quick
     succession. Importantly, this would also provide cost certainty for LSEs and customers.




Vistra Comments Project 58482                                                             Page 9
 8.   To ensure long-term reliability, the new Service must be integrated with ERCOT market
     policies and accurately reflected in Real-Time price formation, particularly through the
     Reliability Deployment Price Adder (RDPA). The RDPA should be reviewed to ensure its
     reasonable accuracy for deployments of the new service and other out-of-market actions.

9.   Vistra recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to implement PURA § 39.170(a)
     and that these protocols should be coordinated with existing load curtailment provisions in
     statutes, PUCT rules, and ERCOT protocols to take into account scenarios where large
     loads will already be curtailed prior to firm load shed.

set a practical limit on the budget for the new Service. The cost could be uplifted to all loads -
so if the fee were set at something like $0.05/MWh, then in a year like 2024 that saw
461.6 TWh of load, the program would have accrued -$23 million that could be used towards
an event-driven procurement; if no event occurred, then the fund would continue to accrue up
to an aggregate limit. Vistra takes no position on the aggregate limit at this time, but highlights
that this approach would favor cost certainty over budget certainty, which may be a more
appropriate step while trying to establish a new service for a largely untested load resource
pool. After a few qualification/procurement rounds, ERCOT will likely be able to better
estimate the willingness of different quantities of load willing to participate each year.



  5.    What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation

market policy framework to mitigate any unintended long-term reliability consequences. Any
deployment associated with the Service needs to be accounted for in Real-Time price formation
through accurate representation in the Reliability Deployment Price Adder (RDPA). Given the

                    VISTRA'S COMMENTS - EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

1.   Vistra suggests the Commission implement an as-needed reliability service under
     PURA § 39.170(b), to be procured when necessary. This meets the goal of minimizing the
     probability of load-shed during anticipated events, while balancing customer cost
     considerations. Vistra also recommends a hybrid funding approach to ensure cost
     certainty and avoid unexpected charges for Load Serving Entities (LSEs) and customers.

2.   PURA § 39.170(b) and (b)(1) together specifically state that the service is to be deployed
     in specified periods in the event of anticipated emergency conditions related to extreme
     weather events.

3.   The Commission should avoid defining "extreme weather event," but guide ERCOT on
     event-based procurement and deployment leveraging existing notification and adjustment
     processes. Vistra suggests procurement be modeled on (and sequenced after, as
     applicable) the Advance Action Notice/Outage Adjustment Evaluation/Outage Scheule
     Adjustment process, possibly in combination with other criteria. Deployment should be
     triggered only after the Commission' s Executive Director has been notified of a potential
     Power Outage Alert under 16 TAC § 25.57(d). These recommendations will help ensure
     efficient, coordinated use of reliability services.

4.   The Commission should not qualify large loads based on whether they require 14 hours to
     ramp down safely, but only whether they are capable of safely ramping down within 24
     hours of a deployment notice.

5.   The Commission should prohibit critical natural gas facilities from participating in the
     new service.

6.   "Participation" in 4CP or a successor transmission cost allocation methodology is too
     narrow in focus and difficult to predict as the Commission is considering changes to that
     methodology. Instead, the Commission should evaluate whether the large load exhibits
     behavior that would hinder its ability to reliably perform during periods when the large
     load may be awarded the new service.

7.   The Target procurement quantity should be based on the available budget and offers
     received. Vistra suggests a "hybrid" approach that uses a consistent, self-leveling fee to
     fund a capped budget pool (but does not opine on the appropriate size of that pool at this
     time). This would allow procurement quantities to be dictated by available funds and
     market offers, and the budget could be subdivided for multiple procurements in quick
     succession. Importantly, this would also provide cost certainty for LSEs and customers.
